pairs.rationale: News that Gentiles received God's word reaches the Judean apostles and brothers; earlier, the Jerusalem apostles heard that Samaria received God's word. The repeated reception-report pattern concerns different communities and episodes.

Peter faces criticism from those of the circumcision in Jerusalem. In Galatians, Cephas withdraws from Gentile meals under circumcision pressure and Paul opposes him in Antioch. These are contrasting disputes about his conduct, not the same visit or critic group.

The Jerusalem objection is that Peter entered uncircumcised men's company and ate with them. Galatians describes Cephas previously eating with Gentiles and then separating himself. The common table-fellowship issue has different actions and challengers.

Peter explicitly explains events in order; Luke explicitly offers an orderly account for Theophilus's certainty. This limited parallel concerns ordered presentation for hearers, without identifying Peter's defense with Luke's written prologue or imposing an exact chronological scheme.
Peter recounts the Joppa prayer, trance and four-cornered descending sheet narrated earlier. The recap says it came right to him; the earlier narrative describes its lowering to the earth.

Peter's inspection of animals in the sheet retells its earlier contents. Both list four-footed animals, creeping things and birds; the recap additionally names wild animals rather than repeating an identical list.
The recalled voice repeats the earlier command to Peter to rise, slaughter and eat. This is Peter's report of the same vision, not a second independently narrated command.
Both reports preserve By no means, Lord, but the earlier account says never eaten anything common and unclean, while the defense says nothing common or unclean has ever entered my mouth.
The second heavenly answer repeats the earlier instruction not to call common what God has cleansed. The link preserves the vision's wording rather than adding a broader food-law ruling.
Both accounts say the event happened three times and the object or contents were taken back into heaven. The earlier narrative adds immediately; the recap says everything was drawn up again.

The three Caesarean messengers reaching the house correspond to Cornelius's men standing at Simon's gate and the Spirit's announcement that three men seek Peter. The recap supplies its own first-person house description.

Both accounts join the Spirit's instruction to accompany the men with brothers accompanying Peter. Acts 10 says without hesitation and some brothers; the recap says making no distinction and specifies six. Their wording and specificity are retained.

Peter repeats the householder's report and the instruction to summon Simon called Peter from Joppa. Cornelius's earlier quoted account describes a man in shining clothing; Peter calls the figure the angel, as the initial narrative also does.

The angel's promised saving message includes the householder and whole household. The jailer is likewise promised salvation in relation to believing in the Lord Jesus, and the word is spoken to everyone in his house. No household ages or unreported individual responses are supplied.

Peter identifies the Gentile Spirit-gift event previously narrated while he was still speaking, including the comparison with the believers' own reception. The recap's as I began and the narrative's while still speaking remain distinct formulations.

Peter's just as upon us at the beginning points back to the community filled with the Holy Spirit at Pentecost. The common Spirit reception does not require the earlier wind-like sound or fire-like tongues to recur in Cornelius's house.

Peter explicitly remembers the Lord's water-versus-Spirit baptism saying, which the opening account records from Jesus. The earlier wording also specifies not many days from now; the remembered excerpt does not.

The same Spirit gift to Gentiles underlies Peter's earlier question about withholding baptismal water and his later question about hindering God. The questions have different immediate objects and occur at different stages of the same affair.

The Jerusalem listeners acknowledge God-granted Gentile repentance leading to life. Peter later argues that God gave Gentiles the Spirit without distinction and that salvation is through Jesus's grace in the same way. The later council is a separate deliberation.

This account explicitly resumes the scattering associated with Stephen's affliction. The earlier narrative recounts his killing, the Jerusalem persecution and scattered believers preaching; this continuation extends the route to Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch.

The supplied text says the Antioch preachers addressed Hellenists with the Lord Jesus's good news; earlier Saul spoke boldly in the Lord's name and disputed with Hellenists in Jerusalem. The shared label is preserved without changing it to Greeks or identifying the two groups.

The Lord's hand accompanies proclamation and many believe here; at Iconium many Jews and Greeks believe while the Lord attests the missionaries' word through signs. These are distinct missions with divine support and widespread response, not identical audiences or a transferred miracle list.

Jerusalem hears of a new community receiving the message and sends a representative to it. The earlier Samaritan report led the apostles to send Peter and John; the Antioch report leads the Church to send Barnabas.

Barnabas urges the Antioch believers to remain with the Lord with steadfast purpose; the later missionary return encourages disciples to remain in the faith. The shared pastoral perseverance instruction has different settings and additional affliction teaching only in the latter.

Barnabas is commended as full of the Holy Spirit and faith; Stephen is similarly called full of faith and the Holy Spirit. The comparison is between the commendations of distinct men, not an identification of Barnabas as one of the Seven.

The brothers had sent Saul to Tarsus when his life was threatened in Jerusalem. Barnabas now goes to Tarsus to seek him, providing a direct narrative location link rather than a new account of Saul's birth or citizenship.

Acts identifies Antioch as the place where disciples were first called Christians; the epistle instructs anyone suffering as a Christian not to be ashamed. The shared designation is concrete, while the epistle does not recount its first use or this year's teaching.

The arrival of prophets at Antioch has a later parallel in Judas and Silas, themselves prophets, encouraging the Antioch brothers with many words. This compares prophetic visits and ministry without assigning those later men's names to the unnamed earlier visitors.

Agabus again appears as a prophet from Judea explicitly speaking through or in the name of the Holy Spirit. His later belt-sign concerns Paul's custody, not the earlier famine or independent confirmation of its extent under Claudius.

The disciples resolve to relieve Judean brothers according to each one's means. The epistle likewise measures acceptable readiness by what one has and directs abundance toward others' lack. The amounts, recipients and occasions are not equated.

Barnabas and Saul carry the relief to the elders; the later unit refers to the same named pair completing their service and taking John called Mark. Its printed returned to Jerusalem is preserved, without replacing it with from Jerusalem or Antioch.

Jesus warns His disciples of being handed over and brought before governors and kings because of Him. Herod's violent action against the Church exemplifies royal persecution; Acts does not narrate a separate formal hearing for every victim.

Mark names James and John, sons of Zebedee, and Jesus speaks of their sharing His cup and baptism. James's killing is a concrete suffering parallel; the saying does not specify his sword-death or narrate John's death.

Herod arrests Peter after seeing that the preceding killing pleased the Jews; earlier the high priest and Sadducees imprisoned the apostles out of jealousy. The repeated apostolic imprisonment has different rulers, motives and prisoner groups.

Herod places Peter under four squads of soldiers; later magistrates order Paul and Silas securely held, and the jailer uses an inner cell and stocks. Both narrate deliberate custody before divine intervention, with distinct security arrangements and no shared Passover date asserted.

The later scene locates many believers praying in Mary the mother of John Mark's house during the same Peter episode. It gives a concrete setting for the Church's prayer without asserting that every Church member was in that single house.

Peter is chained between soldiers before his release; Paul and Silas are in stocks before an earthquake loosens bonds. Peter is sleeping while the later prisoners pray and sing, and their restraints and subsequent actions differ.
An angel of the Lord intervenes in apostolic imprisonment in both episodes. Here light, waking Peter and falling chains are described; the earlier angel opens prison doors and leads the apostles out.

The angel's belt-and-sandals readiness instruction during the Unleavened Bread and Passover setting recalls girded loins, sandals and haste in the Exodus Passover departure. Peter's cloak and the Israelites' staffs remain different items; this is a bounded readiness parallel.

Peter initially thinks the angelic events are a vision and does not know they are real; afterward he explicitly says he now knows the Lord rescued him. The later recognition corrects his initial interpretation within the same narrative.

Peter's iron gate opens of its own accord during the angel-led escape; an earthquake later opens prison doors and loosens bonds. The shared supernatural opening has different means and does not imply that Paul and Silas escaped as Peter did.

Peter acknowledges that the Lord sent His angel and rescued him from royal power. Nebuchadnezzar likewise praises God for sending His angel and saving His servants from fire. The rescue acknowledgment is shared, with different speakers, servants and dangers.

The many praying in John Mark's mother's house give a specific instance of the Church's earnest prayer for imprisoned Peter earlier in the episode. This Mary is identified by her son, without merging her with another Mary or another meeting house.

Both scenes place Peter outside a doorway with a female slave attending it. Rhoda answers his knock at a believing household; John's unnamed doorkeeper participates in his entry into the high priest's courtyard and questions his discipleship. The women are not identified with one another.

Rhoda recognizes Peter's voice and announces that he is outside before opening the gate. The later opening and the group's seeing Peter confirm her specific report, with hearing and seeing assigned to different people.

A woman's unexpected report is initially rejected by a believing group; Luke similarly records the apostles disbelieving the women's tomb report. Peter's prison deliverance is not Jesus's resurrection, and their suggestion about his angel is reported speech rather than a narrated identification.

Opening the door and seeing Peter provide the narrative confirmation of Rhoda's earlier voice-recognition report. The group's astonishment follows its delayed admission rather than disproving that Rhoda had heard the actual Peter.

Peter motions with his hand for silence before relating his deliverance; Paul later motions with his hand and a great silence precedes his address. This is a shared apostolic speech-preface gesture in different gatherings, not the same speech, audience or language claim.

Soldiers are disturbed over Peter's disappearance after guarded imprisonment. Earlier officers find the apostles absent despite locked doors and guards, leaving the temple authorities perplexed. The parallel concerns the unexpected absence and official confusion, not identical prison conditions.

Peter's disappearance leads Herod to order the guards led away for execution. A later jailer, supposing prisoners escaped, prepares to kill himself until Paul stops him. These are contrasting lethal consequences or fears for custodians; neither all guards' completed executions nor an actual later escape is added.

Tyre and Sidon seek peace because their country receives food from Herod's territory. Earlier Hiram of Tyre obtains household loaves, wheat and oil from Solomon amid a timber exchange and peace covenant. This is a bounded Tyrian food-and-royal-peace background, not the same embassy or food arrangement.

The populace calls Herod's voice divine rather than human; the Lystra crowd calls Barnabas and Paul gods in human likeness, which the apostles explicitly reject as fellow humans. The different reactions remain: Acts records Herod's failure to give God glory, not an explicit spoken claim that he is a god.

Herod is struck by an angel, eaten by worms and dies for withholding God's glory. Antiochus is struck by the Lord amid arrogance, suffers worms and decay, and confesses that a mortal must not think himself equal to God. The distinct rulers and bodily details are retained.

Both narrative summaries describe God's word growing. Acts 6 also says disciples increased and many priests obeyed the faith; Acts 12 places the growth summary after Herod's death, without transferring those particular converts to this episode.

John called Mark accompanies Barnabas and Saul here; Barnabas later wants to take the same named companion again, and the dispute ends with Barnabas taking Mark to Cyprus. The comparison does not replace this unit's printed returned to Jerusalem or invent John's reason for leaving the intervening mission.

The earlier Antioch setting places Barnabas and Saul teaching with the Church and records prophets arriving there. The present list supplies additional named prophets and teachers; it does not identify every earlier visitor or equate Lucius with Luke.

The Spirit's call sets Barnabas and Saul apart for work; the earlier Lord-to-Ananias message already chooses Saul to carry His name before Gentiles, kings and Israel. Barnabas is not named in that earlier commission, and the two revelations remain distinct.

Both ministry appointments involve prayer and laying on hands. The Seven are presented to the apostles in Acts 6; the Antioch community fasts and sends Barnabas and Saul away here. The shared actions do not make the roles or appointers identical.

The narrator's sent out by the Holy Spirit directly resumes the Spirit's call and the community's sending after prayer and fasting. Divine commissioning and human sending belong to this same mission, while Seleucia and Cyprus are the ensuing route.

The preceding narrative says Barnabas and Saul took John called Mark with them; the Cyprus mission now has John as an assistant. The continuous party context supplies the companion link without identifying this John with the apostle or making a Gospel-authorship claim.

The magician introduced as the Jewish false prophet Bar-Jesus continues as the proconsul's opposing magician Elymas. The link follows the immediate person-and-role continuity; it does not invent an etymology translating Bar-Jesus into Elymas or identify him with Jesus Christ.

Sergius Paulus first summons the missionaries because he wants God's word; the later proconsul believes and is astonished at the Lord's teaching. This is the same hearer's narrated response, not evidence that Sergius is Saul or that the miracle alone replaces the teaching.

Elymas tries to turn the proconsul away from faith, but the closing account says the proconsul believes. This direct purpose-and-outcome contrast concerns the official's response; it does not narrate Elymas's conversion.

Ananias's earlier message to Saul includes being filled with the Holy Spirit; the narrative now explicitly describes Saul, also called Paul, as Spirit-filled. The connection does not turn the present alias notice into a renaming ceremony at conversion.

Paul combines son-of-the-devil language with deceit in addressing Elymas; Jesus likewise connects devil-parentage with falsehood in addressing His opponents. The comparison concerns these moral characterizations of particular addressees, not biological descent or a blanket ethnic judgment.

Elymas becomes unable to see and seeks hand-leading; Saul earlier could not see and was led by the hand into Damascus. Saul's three days are specified, whereas Elymas's prediction says for a time and no later restoration is narrated here.

The proconsul's belief resolves the earlier contrast between his desire to hear God's word and Elymas's attempt to turn him from faith. The closing emphasis on the Lord's teaching remains alongside what he saw, rather than being reduced to admiration of magic.

The later dispute explicitly recalls John Mark's withdrawal in Pamphylia, corresponding to John's departure from Perga and return to Jerusalem here. Paul's later assessment is reported as his assessment; neither passage supplies John's private reason for leaving.

Paul's entry into the Pisidian Antioch synagogue on the Sabbath parallels his later customary synagogue reasoning at Thessalonica. The later three Sabbaths, city and missionary company are not transferred to this first visit.

Scripture reading in a Sabbath synagogue becomes the occasion for an address in both accounts. Acts names law and prophets and an invitation to encourage; Luke narrates Jesus reading Isaiah and announcing fulfillment, without recording the same invitation or a law reading.

Paul uses a hand gesture before addressing the synagogue audience; later he stands on steps, gestures and addresses a silenced crowd. The formal speech-preface pattern is shared, while Acts 13 does not specify the later Hebrew language or crowd-silence response.

Paul's history joins God's choice, the fathers and Egypt's deliverance by an uplifted arm. Deuteronomy joins Israel's election, the oath to its fathers and redemption from Pharaoh with a mighty hand and uplifted arm. This is related historical-covenant language rather than an identical quotation.

The wilderness summary says God put up with the people's conduct for about forty years; the psalm describes His vexation with a straying generation for forty years. Their conduct-and-duration correspondence is retained without replacing Paul's about with an exact chronology.

Paul looks back on seven Canaanite nations being overthrown and their land inherited. Deuteronomy prospectively names seven nations to be removed as Israel enters its inheritance. The prediction and later summary have different narrative stages.

God's giving judges corresponds to the account of the Lord repeatedly raising judges and rescuing Israel through them. This supports the judges clause, not a calculation assigning the preceding four-hundred-and-fifty-year continuation to the judges' entire duration.

The historical sequence reaches Samuel the prophet; Samuel is explicitly said to judge Israel throughout his life. This supplies his place in the judging history without establishing the four-hundred-and-fifty-year figure or every chronological boundary.

Samuel's selection account identifies Benjamin, Saul son of Kish and the Lord's choice of a king. These match the named king, father and tribe in Paul's summary. The selected Samuel passage does not independently state a forty-year reign.

The beginning of the composite testimony, I have found David, corresponds to the psalm's God-speaking declaration that He found David His servant and anointed him. The psalm does not contain the whole Jesse-and-heart-and-will sentence quoted in Acts.

Samuel announces that the Lord will seek a man according to His heart after Saul's disobedience; Acts applies that description explicitly to David. Samuel's statement does not yet name David, and its third-person wording is not the entire first-person testimony in Acts.

The claim that Jesus comes from David's seed according to promise has concrete Davidic-promise background in God's oath to seat David's bodily offspring on his throne. The psalm itself does not name Jesus or narrate His resurrection.

The announcement to Mary names Jesus and promises Him David's throne and an everlasting reign. Paul's proclamation identifies the promised Davidic Savior as Jesus. The shared named promise does not derive Mary's genealogy from these verses.

Paul summarizes John proclaiming a baptism of repentance before Jesus's coming; Luke narrates John's Jordan-region proclamation of a baptism of repentance for forgiveness. The ministry is John's preparatory work, not John Mark's activity or a claim that it preceded Jesus's birth.

John's denial and unworthiness to untie the coming One's sandals correspond to the Gospel's not-the-Christ declaration and sandal-strap saying. Acts has John asking what others think he is; the Gospel records the envoys' questions. Their dialogue form and questioners are not identical.

Paul renews the speech's twofold address: Israel and God-fearers at the opening, Abraham's family and God-fearers here. This is a repeated audience designation within the same speech, not a claim that every God-fearer is a biological descendant of Abraham.

Both apostolic sermons connect the Jerusalem actors' and rulers' ignorance with fulfillment of the prophets through Christ's suffering. Peter's earlier address and Paul's synagogue sermon are distinct presentations, not a judgment that every Jewish person acted identically.

Luke records Pilate finding no ground for death while the accusers press for crucifixion and their demand is granted. This corresponds to Paul's no-death-cause yet execution-request summary, without claiming that the accusers themselves verbally admitted Pilate's finding.

The removal of Jesus's body and burial correspond to Luke's account of Joseph taking it down and laying it in a tomb. Luke identifies Joseph as a council member who had not consented to the decision; the link does not assign the burial personally to every preceding hostile accuser.

Paul's proclamation that God raised Jesus from the dead repeats Peter's earlier assertion of God raising Him and releasing death's hold. These are shared apostolic resurrection affirmations within Acts, not independently verified modern observations.

The earlier account says Jesus presented Himself alive after suffering and appeared over forty days; Paul likewise speaks of appearances over many days to His companions. Paul's wording does not specify forty here or restrict every resurrection witness to one identical named list.

Paul later again centers his explanation on God's promise to the fathers and hope that includes God raising the dead. The same promise-and-resurrection theme occurs in a trial rather than this synagogue proclamation, with different hearers and circumstances.

Acts explicitly identifies the second psalm and quotes the Lord's sonship-and-today-begetting declaration. The supplied psalm has You are My son where Acts has Thou art My Son; the correspondence is preserved without treating the English forms as identical or replacing raising up with extra words.

The holy and sure blessings of David come from Isaiah's everlasting-covenant promise. Acts uses this promise within its argument for Jesus's resurrection and no return to decay; Isaiah's invitation and covenant wording do not themselves explicitly narrate that resurrection.

The Holy One's not seeing decay corresponds to the psalm's promise not to let the holy one see corruption, alongside not abandoning the soul to Hades. Acts applies the cited promise to the raised Jesus; the supplied decay and corruption renderings are retained.

Both sermons distinguish David's death and burial from the resurrection promise concerning Christ. Paul adds serving his generation and seeing decay; Peter mentions the tomb and prophetic foresight. Their related argument is not an identical account of all details.

Peter likewise joins Christ's flesh not seeing decay with God raising Jesus. Paul contrasts the raised One with David's decay in the preceding unit. Both affirm the resurrection reading of the promise without providing a new independent inspection of either body.

Forgiveness of sins proclaimed through Jesus corresponds to Peter's promise of forgiveness through His name for everyone believing in Him. This target supports the forgiveness clause; Paul's law-and-justification contrast continues grammatically into the next unit.

Both passages connect justification with believing in Christ rather than law as its basis. Acts speaks of everything from which one could not be justified in Moses's law; Galatians states its works-of-law contrast explicitly. The related formulations are not rewritten into one identical sentence.

This introduction to the following prophetic warning is concretely anchored by the scoffers/despisers, marveling and unbelievable-work wording quoted next. Habakkuk's own setting announces the Chaldeans, rather than explicitly narrating the present resurrection proclamation.

The warning shares the despisers or scoffers address, marvel-and-vanish command and work unbelieved even when reported. Acts has a shorter adapted formulation; the Greek-edition Habakkuk says despisers rather than replacing it with a different edition's among-the-nations wording.

The request to hear these words on the next Sabbath is followed by the coming-Sabbath gathering to hear the Lord's word. The latter's almost-whole-city attendance is its own expanded audience description, not a statement that every requester or attendee believed.

Paul and Barnabas urge those following them to remain in God's grace; Barnabas earlier encouraged Antioch believers to remain with the Lord after seeing God's grace. Pisidian Antioch and the earlier commissioning community's Antioch are distinct settings.

The coming-Sabbath gathering follows the earlier explicit request for these words on the next Sabbath. This links the requested hearing with its narrated occasion, preserving almost the whole city rather than asserting the entire city converted.

Jealousy prompts opposition to the apostolic mission in both episodes. The earlier high priest's Sadducee party imprisons apostles; the present opponents contradict Paul abusively. These groups, actions and places differ, and Jews who followed the missionaries earlier are not included automatically among these opponents.

Paul later responds to abusive opposition while witnessing to Jews by announcing a turn to Gentiles. Both are local missionary responses; neither comparison turns them into a permanent abandonment of every Jewish hearer, since the narrative continues synagogue ministry.

The light-for-nations and salvation-to-earth's-end commission corresponds to Isaiah's servant saying. Acts explicitly applies the command to us in the missionary speech; Isaiah's fuller wording also concerns Jacob, Israel's dispersion and a covenant, not Paul and Barnabas named there.

Gentile inclusion is associated with life and praise in both accounts. Here Gentiles rejoice, glorify the word and believe with appointed-to-life wording; the earlier Jerusalem listeners glorify God for Gentile repentance leading to life. The different subjects and formulations do not yield an added predestination scheme.

Both summaries describe the Lord's word reaching a broad region through missionary proclamation. The later account specifies two years and Asia's Jewish and Greek residents; those duration and geographical details are not assigned to the present whole-region report.

Jewish opponents mobilize local people and civic influence against missionaries in both episodes. Acts 17 names a mob, Jason and city officials, while this account names devout high-standing women, leading men and expulsion. It does not give the same actors or identical departure mechanism.

The missionaries' shaking dust from their feet against the rejecting group follows the concrete mission-response pattern Jesus instructed when a city did not receive His messengers. The Lukan instruction initially addresses the Twelve, not a claim that Paul and Barnabas were in that original group.

The disciples' joy and Holy Spirit filling close a persecution episode; the Thessalonians receive the word in great affliction with joy from the Holy Spirit. The passages associate joy with the Spirit amid opposition in different communities; only the epistle explicitly describes the joy as from the Spirit. This does not identify every disciple here with the departing pair.

The synagogue mission addresses both Jews and Greeks in each account. Iconium has a great multitude believing, whereas the later Corinth account says Paul sought to persuade them every Sabbath. The outcome and missionary company are not made identical.

Unbelieving opponents stir hostility against the mission; later Thessalonian Jews also stir and disturb crowds when Paul's word reaches Berea. The latter is another city's opposition, not an assertion that the Jewish believers just named in Iconium opposed their own faith.

The Lord attests the word of grace with signs and wonders through the missionaries; Hebrews likewise describes God bearing witness to the saving proclamation through signs, wonders and mighty deeds. Hebrews does not name this Iconium episode or these particular agents.

Iconium's city population divides between the opponents and apostles; Paul's later listeners divide between persuasion and disbelief and disagree with one another. The common divided response has different social scale and groups, not a claim that all Jewish people belong to one unbelieving side.

An earlier attempt seeks to stone the missionaries; later opponents from Antioch and Iconium persuade a crowd and Paul is actually stoned at Lystra. The later violence does not mean the earlier city's attempt was completed or that Barnabas was also stoned.

Learning of the persecution attempt, the missionaries flee to other cities. Jesus's instruction likewise says to flee from one persecuting city to another. Its accompanying saying about Israel's cities and the Son of Man is not used to date this journey.

The missionaries continue good-news proclamation after fleeing persecution; earlier scattered believers likewise go about proclaiming the word as good news. The shared movement-and-continued-preaching pattern concerns different groups and stages of the mission.

Both healing accounts introduce a man unable to walk from his mother's womb. The Jerusalem man is carried to beg at the temple gate; the Lystra man is said never to have walked. The men and locations remain distinct.

Paul's intent look before healing parallels Peter and John's intent look at the other birth-disabled man. Acts 14 explicitly says Paul recognized healing faith; Acts 3 instead describes attention and an expectation of receiving something, not that same explicit pre-healing faith statement.

An apostolic command is followed by a previously disabled man leaping and walking in both episodes. Peter explicitly uses Jesus's name and lifts by the right hand; Paul's quoted command here is stand upright, without those additional narrated actions.

The crowd mistakes a sign involving Paul for evidence of divinity; islanders later likewise call Paul a god after he suffers no harm. These are the onlookers' interpretations, with gods in human likeness here and no Zeus or Hermes naming in the later verse.

The crowd's Zeus-and-Hermes labels are directly answered by the named apostles Barnabas and Paul declaring themselves fellow human beings. The report of what the crowd called them is not the narrator's endorsement that they are gods.

The priest and crowd want to sacrifice to the missionaries; the later statement says the apostles' words scarcely stop the crowds from sacrificing. This is the same attempted rite and its restrained outcome, not an apostolically approved offering.

The apostles tear garments before rejecting divine identification in a healing setting; Israel's king tears garments and asks Am I God when asked to cure Naaman. The common gesture and God-human distinction have different motives: refusal of worship here, political alarm about the letter there.

Peter raises Cornelius after he bows before him and says he too is human; Barnabas and Paul likewise answer the attempted sacrifice by asserting shared humanity. Bowing at feet and offering sacrifice are different actions, not a declaration that every gesture of respect is identical.

The living God's making heaven, earth, sea and everything in them closely matches the psalm's Creator formula. Acts does not name the psalm as its exclusive source, and its call to turn from worthless things is the missionary speech's own setting.

The Gentile addresses describe earlier divine forbearance before the present call to turn to God: allowing nations their ways here, overlooking times of ignorance and now commanding repentance later. The wording and fuller Athens argument remain distinct.

Both give God credit for watering the earth and producing food associated with human gladness. The psalm specifies plants, bread, wine and oil; Acts speaks of heavenly rains and fruitful seasons. The common providence does not make their lists identical.

Acts says God's beneficial rain-witness continued while nations went their own ways; Jesus likewise says the Father sends rain on righteous and unrighteous. The shared providence extends beyond the faithful without identifying every nation or hearer as one moral category.

The apostles' words scarcely stop the sacrifice that the priest and crowd had wanted to offer earlier. The specific attempted offering supplies the antecedent for this outcome, while the passage never presents it as worship accepted by the missionaries.

Paul's letter recalls being stoned once, providing a close personal-suffering parallel to the concrete Lystra stoning. The letter does not name Lystra or describe the dragging and presumed death; Acts itself says the attackers supposed him dead.

Paul getting up after the stoning and continuing his mission illustrates the letter's struck down but not destroyed contrast. Acts reports the attackers' supposition of death, not an explicit declaration that disciples raised a dead Paul; the letter does not name this incident.

The earlier flight brought the missionaries to Lystra and Derbe, where they continued preaching. After evangelizing Derbe, they return to Lystra, Iconium and Antioch. This connects outward and returning stages of the same journey while preserving the differing place lists, without treating the link as an independent map or merging the two Antiochs.

The letter recalls persecutions at Antioch, Iconium and Lystra and says godly life in Christ entails persecution. The missionary return to these communities likewise teaches perseverance through afflictions toward God's kingdom, without making suffering a payment that earns entry.

The missionary appointment of elders in each Church parallels the instruction that Titus appoint elders in every Cretan city. The locations and recipients differ; prayer and fasting are narrated in Acts, not repeated in the selected Titus instruction.

The earlier outward route goes through Perga in Pamphylia toward Pisidian Antioch; the returning mission now traverses Pisidia toward Pamphylia. The shared regions and reversed travel stage are explicit, without supplying unrecorded roads or dates.

Perga, where John had left the outward mission, is now a place where the returning missionaries speak the word. This is a concrete return-location link; the earlier unit does not attest Attalia, this preaching, or John's rejoining the party.

The return to the Antioch where they were entrusted to grace explicitly closes the work begun with the Spirit's call and the Church's sending. This is the commissioning community's Antioch, distinct from the Pisidian mission stop, with the same work now described as completed.

God opening a door of faith to Gentiles parallels Paul's door opened in the Lord when he came to Troas for Christ's good news. Both use an opened-door mission metaphor; the letter describes an opportunity and does not repeat this entire Gentile-conversion report.

The same pair's later remaining at Antioch with teaching and proclamation parallels the present extended stay with disciples after the mission. These are different intervals around the Jerusalem consultation, and the later verse supplies no exact duration for this earlier stay.

deferred.reason: The appointed day, royal clothing, tribunal and public address have no sufficiently specific retained counterpart. General scenes of rulers in ceremonial dress would give only a loose resemblance for this unit.

review_notes: Pinned Saints original cache: 328967336f32958587835c921fea3b96a5bf6494. Every Acts 11–12 original unit was read in a complete small chapter display; every retained target and relevant context was read after the complete assigned-source reread. All displayed read groups were complete and below the outer output limit.
Internal recaps, explicit report confirmations and formal narrative parallels are labeled as such, not counted as independent historical witnesses.
Preserve Hellenists at 11:20, making no distinction at 11:12, returned to Jerusalem at 12:25, and the different animal lists at 11:6/10:12. No Saints wording, numbering or continuation was changed.

Mary is identified as John Mark's mother; Rhoda is not merged with John's unnamed doorkeeper. The living James named12:17 is not equated with the James killed12:2. The angel claim at 12:15 and divine-voice claim at 12:22 remain the speakers' claims.

The Old Testament targets use actual supplied Greek-edition numbering, including Daniel 3:95 and1Kings5:23–26. Their correspondences are bounded and do not establish medical identity or a second attestation of Herod's embassy.

The complete primary scope is Acts 11–14: 135 original units. Chapter 15's preparatory source-only reading receives zero completed-source credit; later Acts passages retained here are targets or context, and the next source boundary remains Acts 15:1.

Acts 13–14 sources were read in complete individual chapter displays, followed by every retained target with relevant actual context in complete small groups. The final Acts 13–14 context view contained 82 units/2643 tokens and was complete; other target groups were smaller.

Preserve the original continuations at 13:19–20,13:23–24,13:38–39 and14:14–15. The 450-year phrase is not reassigned to a judges-only chronology. The selected Samuel passage does not corroborate Saul's forty-year reign.

Saul also called Paul is an alias notice, not a narrated conversion renaming or derivation from Sergius Paulus. Bar-Jesus/Elymas remains the specific magician; no new etymology is supplied. John Mark the assistant is distinct from John the baptism preacher.
